terms.Learning-rate schedule: Warmup (a linear ramp over the first few hundred to few thousand steps) protects the randomly initialized network while Adam's second-moment estimates are still noisy. Decay then follows cosine, linear-to-zero, step decay, or warmup-stable-decay (WSD), which holds the peak and anneals over the last 10-20% of steps. Cosine is tied to the planned run length T, so stopping early leaves the model under-annealed; WSD lets you branch a decay from any checkpoint, which helps scaling-law sweeps and continued pretraining. The peak learning rate is the most important hyperparameter; muP helps transfer it across model widths.
terms.Vanishing gradients: The gradient at an early layer is a product of per-layer Jacobians, so its size scales roughly with the product of their singular values. Sigmoid's derivative is at most 0.25, so ten sigmoid layers can shrink a gradient by about 1e-6; in RNNs the same recurrent matrix repeats at every step, which makes both vanishing and exploding worse. Diagnose with per-layer gradient-norm logging. Remedies: variance-preserving initialization (Xavier, He), non-saturating activations, normalization layers, residual connections (the identity term in I + dF/dx), gating in LSTMs and GRUs, and gradient clipping for the exploding case.
terms.Batch normalization: BatchNorm computes y = gamma * (x - mu_B) / sqrt(var_B + eps) + beta per channel; for conv features the statistics run over batch, height and width. It keeps running averages for inference, so model.train() and model.eval() really behave differently. Small batches give noisy statistics, and multi-GPU training may need SyncBatchNorm. Its original 'internal covariate shift' motivation is disputed; later evidence suggests it smooths the loss landscape, allowing larger learning rates. A conv bias before BatchNorm is redundant. When fine-tuning with small batches, freeze its statistics or switch to GroupNorm.
terms.Layer normalization: LayerNorm normalizes over the feature dimension of each token, so a (B, T, D) tensor gets B*T separate statistics over D values, and training and inference behave identically. It never mixes information across examples or time steps, which suits autoregressive models. RMSNorm (2019) drops mean-centering and the bias, computing x / sqrt(mean(x^2) + eps) * g; it is cheaper and standard in Llama-family and most current LLMs. Pre-norm placement (normalize before each sublayer) trains deep stacks more reliably than post-norm. QK-norm applies the same idea to queries and keys to stop attention logits from growing.
terms.Residual connection: Introduced in ResNet (He et al., 2015) to fix the degradation problem, where deeper plain networks had higher training error than shallower ones. The Jacobian of x + F(x) is I + dF/dx, so gradients always have an identity path. Shape changes use 1x1 projection shortcuts. Because each block adds to the stream, variance grows with depth; remedies include zero-initializing the last layer of each branch, scaling branch outputs by about 1/sqrt(2N), and DeepNorm. Stochastic depth drops whole residual blocks at random during training. In transformers, residual connections form the residual stream that interpretability work studies.
terms.Dropout: Inverted dropout multiplies surviving activations by 1/(1 - p) at training time so inference needs no rescaling. Typical rates: 0.5 in old fully connected layers, about 0.1 in transformers, and often 0 in single-epoch LLM pretraining, where overfitting is minimal. It can be read as training an exponential ensemble of thinned networks that share weights. Recurrent connections need the same mask at every step (variational dropout). Monte Carlo dropout, which keeps dropout on at test time and averages several passes, gives a rough uncertainty estimate. Dropout before BatchNorm can cause a train/test variance mismatch.
terms.Convolutional neural network: A conv layer's weight has shape (C_out, C_in, k, k), and the output size per dimension is floor((n + 2p - k)/s) + 1. Weight sharing and local connectivity give translation equivariance and parameter counts that do not depend on image size. Receptive fields grow with depth and stride. Key lineage: LeNet-5 (1998), AlexNet (2012), VGG (2014), Inception, ResNet (2015), MobileNet, EfficientNet, and ConvNeXt (2022), which showed modernized CNNs can match vision transformers. CNNs remain strong for edge devices and dense high-resolution prediction, and diffusion U-Nets are built from conv blocks.
terms.Recurrent neural network: A vanilla RNN updates h_t = tanh(W_h h_(t-1) + W_x x_t + b) and trains with backpropagation through time, which stores every step and suffers vanishing gradients. The LSTM adds a cell state updated additively, c_t = f*c_(t-1) + i*c~_t, so the gradient along it scales by the forget gate f; the GRU merges cell and hidden state with update and reset gates and about 25% fewer parameters. RNNs have constant per-step inference cost but cannot train in parallel over time. Modern state-space models such as Mamba revive recurrence with parallel-scan training.
terms.Cosine similarity: cos(a, b) = a.b / (|a| |b|). For unit-normalized vectors it equals the dot product, and squared Euclidean distance equals 2 - 2*cos, so all three produce the same ranking; systems normalize once and use fast inner-product search. Absolute values are model-specific: many embedders are anisotropic, so unrelated texts can score 0.6-0.8 and thresholds must be calibrated per model. High cosine means similar context and topic, not agreement or relevance: opposite-sentiment sentences often score high. Without normalization, dot products favor long vectors, such as popular items in recommenders.
terms.Variational autoencoder: A VAE maximizes the evidence lower bound (ELBO), E_q[log p(x|z)] - KL(q(z|x) || p(z)), with a Gaussian encoder q, a standard-normal prior and the reparameterization z = mu + sigma*eps so gradients reach the encoder. The KL term has a closed form for Gaussians. Gaussian decoders produce blurry samples because they average over plausible outputs; strong decoders can cause posterior collapse, where z is ignored. Variants include beta-VAE for disentanglement and VQ-VAE with discrete codebooks. Today VAEs mainly serve as compressors: latent diffusion runs in a VAE's latent space.
terms.Generative adversarial network: GANs solve min over G, max over D of E[log D(x)] + E[log(1 - D(G(z)))]; in practice the generator uses the non-saturating loss, maximizing log D(G(z)). With an optimal discriminator the objective relates to the Jensen-Shannon divergence. Training is a two-player game that can oscillate; stabilizers include Wasserstein losses with gradient penalty, spectral normalization and two-timescale learning rates. Mode collapse means covering only a few modes of the data. StyleGAN set the photorealism bar in 2019; today adversarial losses mainly sharpen image tokenizers, super-resolution and few-step diffusion distillation.
terms.Diffusion model: DDPM-style training samples a noise level t, forms x_t = sqrt(abar_t) x_0 + sqrt(1 - abar_t) eps in closed form, and regresses the noise with an MSE loss; this is equivalent to learning the score (the gradient of log density) at each noise level. Sampling integrates the reverse process with solvers such as DDIM or DPM-Solver in 20-50 steps, or 1-4 after distillation or with consistency models. Classifier-free guidance trades diversity for prompt adherence. Latent diffusion works in a VAE latent space; flow matching and diffusion transformers (DiT) underpin many current image and video models.
